o: With |s| ≤ 10 there are at most 55 substrings, each parsing to a number below 10¹⁰ (fits in 64-bit). Collect the distinct parsed values, keep the primes, sort descending, and sum the top three (or all if fewer). Leading zeros vanish automatically through integer parsing ("05" → 5). Example 1: primes {2,3,23,223,1223} → 1223+223+23 = 1469; Example 2: only 11 → 11.
k: Only ≤ 55 substrings exist, so generating and testing each individually is cheap.
Values fit in 64-bit integers; trial division up to √x (~10⁵) is fast enough, though Miller–Rabin is cleaner.
Deduplicate before summing — repeated substrings count once.

a.i: Generate every substring, parse to an integer into a set, test each with trial division, sort the primes descending and take three.
s: Collect int(s[i:j]) for all 0 ≤ i < j ≤ n into a set.
Filter primality by trial division up to √x.
Sort descending, sum the first min(3, count) primes.
a.t: O(k² · √M) where k = |s| ≤ 10 and M < 10¹⁰ — at most 55 numbers each tested in ~10⁵ divisions.
a.sp: O(k²) — the set of distinct values.

a.i: Same enumeration, but primality is decided by deterministic Miller–Rabin with the witness set {2,...,37}, which is exact for all 64-bit inputs and runs in O(log³ M) per number.
s: Sort descending and sum the top three primes.
a.t: O(k² · log³ M) — Miller–Rabin per candidate with k ≤ 10 substrings.
a.sp: O(k²) — the set of distinct values.

w: Trial division is perfectly adequate given |s| ≤ 10; mention Miller–Rabin as the scalable alternative. Pitfalls: forgetting deduplication ("22" yields 2 twice), mishandling leading zeros (integer parsing handles them), and 1 not being prime. Follow-ups: sum of k largest primes for long strings (needs rolling substrings + a primality sieve up to the max feasible value), or count distinct prime substrings.
